text:
Rep: Wren, Linnea, thanks for taking my call.
Wren Underhill (Operations Manager): Hi. We're going to be quick. We've decided on Tallyhold.
Rep: Okay. May I ask what led to it?
Wren Underhill (Operations Manager): Our broker. That's the plain version. She handles our benefits renewals, has for years, and she sent us their bundle. Payroll, benefits, the lot. That's what she put in front of us.
Linnea Delacroix (COO): We trust her. She's saved us money on carriers more than once.
Wren Underhill (Operations Manager): I'm not going to pretend I did a full bake-off. We saw your demo, it was fine, but at the end of the day the person who handles our renewals recommended the other one. It seemed silly to fight her.
Linnea Delacroix (COO): Compliance-wise, she vouched for them too.
Rep: Was there anything we could have done differently?
Wren Underhill (Operations Manager): Not really. We just went with her advice.
Rep: I understand. Thank you for being direct.
Wren Underhill (Operations Manager): Of course. Best of luck.

Rep: Kofi, Annelise, good morning, and thank you for joining.
Kofi Santangelo (VP of People): Good morning. I shall be brief, as I do not wish to waste your time. We have chosen to proceed with Brasswick Payroll.
Rep: I appreciate you telling me. May I ask what influenced the decision?
Kofi Santangelo (VP of People): The timing, principally. Our first conversation was on the third. The demonstration did not take place until the fourteenth. Eleven days. In that period, Brasswick provided a full walk-through, answered our written questions, and sent a draft contract.
Annelise Vasquez (HR Director): I would add that our leadership asked for a decision before the end of the quarter. We had no way of holding the process open while we waited for a second demonstration.
Kofi Santangelo (VP of People): By the time your team arrived, the matter had, in effect, been settled internally. I regret that, because your presentation was thorough. I would have given it a fair hearing a week earlier.
Annelise Vasquez (HR Director): It was thorough, yes.
Rep: Thank you. If circumstances change, we would be glad to speak again.
Kofi Santangelo (VP of People): Certainly. Thank you for your courtesy throughout.
Annelise Vasquez (HR Director): Thank you.

Rep: Casper, Odalys, thanks for getting on the line. How are things?
Casper Nakamura (Office Manager): Good, good. Busy, as ever. I wanted to touch base, and I figured a call was better than an email.
Rep: Appreciate that. How did the team feel after the demo?
Casper Nakamura (Office Manager): Everyone was positive about the session. Very professional. Odalys, you were on that too.
Odalys Zeller (COO): I was. It was well done. Thank you for the effort.
Casper Nakamura (Office Manager): So I'll just say it. We've decided to go a different direction.
Rep: I see. Can I ask what you're leaning toward, or what drove the choice?
Casper Nakamura (Office Manager): I'd rather not get into it. It's nothing dramatic. We just made a change, and we wanted to let you know right away.
Odalys Zeller (COO): Yes. No bad blood at all. We'll recommend you to people if it comes up.
Rep: That's kind of you. If anything shifts, the door's open.
Casper Nakamura (Office Manager): Understood. We appreciate that.
Odalys Zeller (COO): Thanks again, and good luck with the rest of the year.
Rep: Same to you both.

Rep: Oriel, Ingrid, thanks for joining. I've got your note.
Oriel Eastwood (Chief People Officer): Yes. I'll be direct. We're going with Tallyhold.
Rep: Understood. What tipped it?
Oriel Eastwood (Chief People Officer): Our broker. She does our benefits renewals. Has for years. She brought us the bundle. We looked at it. It's what she put in front of us.
Ingrid Galbraith (COO): Four hundred ninety-three people. Eleven states. We don't have time to build our own comparison. She knows our carriers, our history.
Oriel Eastwood (Chief People Officer): I trust her. Simple as that. When she says this is the one, I listen.
Rep: Was there a gap in our offer?
Oriel Eastwood (Chief People Officer): No. Your demo was solid. Your team was responsive. This isn't about you.
Ingrid Galbraith (COO): It's about who we trust to handle the renewals.
Oriel Eastwood (Chief People Officer): Exactly. Short sentences. Clean decision.
Rep: Thank you for being clear.
Ingrid Galbraith (COO): Take care.

Subject: Our decision

Hi,

Thanks for your time and for the demos. We've decided to go with Tallyhold.

Our benefits broker, who manages our renewals, recommended their bundle and we are following her advice. It was not a reflection on Lanternmere or your team.

We appreciate the professionalism.

Oriel

Rep: Beatrix, Delphine, hello. Thank you both for joining.
Beatrix Moreau (COO): Good afternoon. Thank you for taking the time. I will not keep you long. We have reached a decision, and we thought it only courteous to tell you ourselves.
Delphine Galbraith (CFO): Yes, good afternoon.
Beatrix Moreau (COO): We have decided to make a change, and we are going in a different direction. I want to say that your team has been generous with its time.
Rep: Thank you. May I ask anything that would help us understand?
Beatrix Moreau (COO): I would prefer to leave it there, if you do not mind. It is not a matter I can explain at length.
Delphine Galbraith (CFO): We thought the process was well run.
Beatrix Moreau (COO): One small aside, if I may, as you will want to know. During our trial, the mobile app logged our supervisors out each time the phone locked. One of them had to sign in four times in a single morning to approve timesheets. I mention it only in passing.
Rep: That is useful, and I will pass it on to the team.
Beatrix Moreau (COO): Thank you. But it is not the reason. As I say, we have simply made a change.
Delphine Galbraith (CFO): With our thanks.
Rep: And with mine. Goodbye.

Rep: Odalys, Lucian, thanks for dialling in. I know you've got a lot on.
Odalys Moreau (Office Manager): I do. I've got eight states' worth of payroll in my head and I'm tired. So let me ask what I've been asking since the start. Taxes.
Rep: State and local.
Odalys Moreau (Office Manager): Yes. Take our guy in Pennsylvania. Lives in Pennsylvania, works in New Jersey, and then moved to Delaware in June. What does your system do? Last time, you said, and I wrote it down, 'we'd have to check on the reciprocity piece.'
Lucian Quillfeather (COO): And then there's the local piece. We've got people in Ohio cities that have their own income tax. Who files that? You, or us?
Rep: I believe we handle the registrations in most states, but let me confirm the local filings with the tax team.
Lucian Quillfeather (COO): See, 'I believe.' We can't run on that. If one filing is wrong, it's a penalty, and it's my signature.
Odalys Moreau (Office Manager): I'm not worried about price. I'd say it was about what we pay now, within a couple thousand. Fine. I just need a system that can tell me, with a straight face, that the mid-year move is handled.
Lucian Quillfeather (COO): And the demo took, what, eleven days to schedule? Not the issue. But it didn't help.
Rep: Understood.
Odalys Moreau (Office Manager): We're going to Brasswick. They had the answers.

Subject: Closing the loop

Hi,

Thanks for your time and for being honest about what you'd need to confirm. We've decided to go with Corvane.

The deciding point was state and local payroll tax handling. Across eight states, we needed firm answers on reciprocity, mid-year moves and local filings, and we didn't get them with confidence. Cost was not the reason.

The eleven days before the demo was a minor frustration, nothing more.

Thank you again,
Odalys

Rep: Maren, Calla, thanks for hopping on.
Maren Valdivia (COO): Sure, sure. So, I was telling Calla before you joined, I've been thinking about this out loud all weekend. Basically, the demo was great, the people were great, and I kept coming back to the same thing, which is the tax question. And it's not a small one, because we're in five states.
Calla Whitlock (HR Director): Five, yes.
Maren Valdivia (COO): So the example I keep thinking about. We have a few hotel staff who live in Kentucky and work across the river in Ohio. And I asked, and I think, was it you? Someone said, 'we'd have to check on whether we withhold for both.' And I thought, well, that's the whole job, isn't it? I mean, that's what I'm paying for.
Calla Whitlock (HR Director): And the other was local taxes. We had a case in Pennsylvania where one township takes a bit of a per-head tax, and I asked how it gets registered, and the answer was kind of, we'll get back to you.
Maren Valdivia (COO): And you did get back to us, to be fair, a week later. But a week is a week. I don't want to be that person learning during year one.
Calla Whitlock (HR Director): The price, honestly, was fine. A bit higher than Corvane, sure, but I'd have paid it.
Maren Valdivia (COO): Right, if I'd felt solid. But I didn't, and I think I'd rather have it right. So we're going with Corvane. Sorry!
Rep: Thanks for being straight.

Rep: Beatrix, Idris, good afternoon. Thank you for joining me.
Beatrix Cadogan (Head of HR): Good afternoon. I will be candid, and I hope you will take it constructively. We have decided not to proceed.
Rep: I would value hearing the reasons.
Beatrix Cadogan (Head of HR): The principal concern is payroll tax. We have employees in six states. In our second session I asked what happens when an employee moves from Maryland to Virginia in the middle of the year, and the response was that the team would have to check. I then asked how reciprocity between Washington, D.C. and its neighbours is handled for a remote worker, and the answer, again, was that you would confirm.
Idris Ivarsson (General Manager): Those are not exotic situations for us. They occur every quarter. I need an answer that does not begin with 'I will find out.'
Beatrix Cadogan (Head of HR): The follow-up arrived, but it was general. It did not tell us who is responsible for the registrations.
Idris Ivarsson (General Manager): Cost was not a concern. I will mention it only because you will ask. The figure was within our range, and I have no complaint about it.
Beatrix Cadogan (Head of HR): There was a lag of nine days before the demonstration, which was less than ideal, but it is not material.
Rep: I understand. Which direction are you going?
Beatrix Cadogan (Head of HR): Corvane. Their answers were specific.
Idris Ivarsson (General Manager): We wish you well.

Rep: Yuki, Ravi, thanks for jumping on.
Yuki Valdivia (Chief People Officer): Hi. Let's get to it. Ravi, you want to start?
Ravi Petrakis (HR Director): Sure. We've decided on Brasswick. The reason is taxes. We have people in nine states, and the thing I kept asking was how you handle state unemployment registrations when we add a state. Your answer was, 'we'd have to check what the onboarding team does.' That's not an answer for me.
Yuki Valdivia (Chief People Officer): And mine was a specific case. We have a warehouse supervisor who lives in Indiana, works in Kentucky, and picks up shifts in Ohio now and then. Which state's tax comes out, and who files the return? Same story. We'd need to look into it.
Rav: Right.
Ravi Petrakis (HR Director): Brasswick walked through it on the call. State by state. Gave us a document.
Yuki Valdivia (Chief People Officer): Price. It came up once. We were comfortable with yours. If you'd had the tax answers, I'd have paid it.
Rep: Did you want me to bring in someone from our tax team for a follow-up?
Yuki Valdivia (Chief People Officer): That was offered, and I appreciate it. But we're at day ten from the first call, and my CEO wants a decision.
Ravi Petrakis (HR Director): We signed yesterday.
Rep: Understood. Thanks for the clear feedback.
Yuki Valdivia (Chief People Officer): Of course. Good luck.

Rep: Signe, Emeka, hi. Thanks for getting on.
Signe Fonseca (Office Manager): Hi. I'll say upfront I'm worn out, so I'm just going to say what I think. We're going with Tallyhold.
Emeka Ibarra (Head of People): It came down to taxes, mostly. We're in four states and there's a lot of back and forth. People who live in one and work in another. Signe asked on the demo, what if someone lives in Maryland but works in D.C., what gets withheld. And the answer was, 'we'd have to check.'
Signe Fonseca (Office Manager): And then I asked about a guy who moved from Virginia to North Carolina in August. How do you split the year. Same answer. 'We'd have to check.' I wanted someone to say, here's what happens.
Emeka Ibarra (Head of People): Tallyhold had it laid out.
Signe Fonseca (Office Manager): Price wasn't it. Yours was a little higher, but nothing I'd lose sleep over.
Emeka Ibarra (Head of People): Our broker also likes Tallyhold, and she does our renewals, so that nudged things. But if your tax side had been solid, I think we'd have stuck with you.
Signe Fonseca (Office Manager): Yeah. It's the tax thing. I'm sorry.
Rep: No need. Thank you for telling me.
Emeka Ibarra (Head of People): It was a good demo otherwise.

Rep: Rafferty, Greta, thanks for the time.
Rafferty Fairweather (COO): I'll be quick. Five states, 437 people, and I need payroll taxes to be handled without me thinking about them. That's the whole thing.
Rep: Understood.
Rafferty Fairweather (COO): So here's what I asked. One. Driver based in Tennessee, delivers into Georgia and Alabama. Which state is the withholding for? Your answer was, 'we'd have to confirm with our compliance people.' Two. A dispatcher in our Nashville office moves to Atlanta in July. Do I register in Georgia that day? Same answer, more or less.
Greta Parekh (CFO): And I wrote a question list for you after the demo. We got half of it back. The half we got was fine. The other half, I'm still waiting for.
Rafferty Fairweather (COO): I don't think it's about price. Your number was around what I expected. Corvane is a little less, but I'd have paid more for certainty.
Greta Parekh (CFO): Candidly, we've also slowed things down. Our board's talking about holding off on any big system change until the sale of the Memphis yard is done. So even with perfect answers, the timing wouldn't have been great.
Rafferty Fairweather (COO): That's secondary. The tax question is why I'm leaning Corvane.
Rep: Anything I can do to change that?
Rafferty Fairweather (COO): Get me real answers in writing by Friday. Otherwise, we're done.
Greta Parekh (CFO): He means it.

Rep: Fenella, Teodoro, hi. Thanks for joining, both of you.
Fenella Santangelo (HR Director): Hi! Yes. Okay. So, I'll try to be organised, but I'm going to ramble, bear with me. First, I want to say the team was lovely. Teodoro, you agree?
Teodoro Santangelo (Operations Director): Very nice people, yes.
Fenella Santangelo (HR Director): So, the thing. We're in eight states. Eight! Which sounds like a lot, but it's mostly small clusters, two people here, three there. And I started asking about payroll taxes, and it's not that you didn't know, it's that, well, every time it got to anything specific, someone said they'd have to check.
Teodoro Santangelo (Operations Director): Like the one about Montana. We've got two remote folks in Montana and I asked how you register the state account. And I got a very nice answer that boiled down to 'I'll find out.'
Fenella Santangelo (HR Director): And mine was a lady who lives in Oregon and works from home but her employer, that's us, is in Washington, and then she moved to Idaho in June. What happens to the year? And I got another 'let me check.' Which, you know, I do appreciate honesty, I'd rather that than a wrong answer.
Teodoro Santangelo (Operations Director): The price was fine. I want to say that. It's about what Brasswick wanted.
Fenella Santangelo (HR Director): Right, right. If I'd felt covered, I'd have signed it. But Brasswick just seemed to have it down. They had a woman on the call who'd done nothing but multi-state filings for fifteen years.
Rep: That makes sense. Thank you both.
Fenella Santangelo (HR Director): Thank you for taking it so well!

Subject: Thanks, and where we landed

Hi,

Thank you for all your help, and for being so honest when you didn't know an answer. We've decided to go with Brasswick Payroll.

The deciding factor was multi-state payroll tax handling. With employees in eight states, we needed specifics on registrations and mid-year moves, and they had them ready. Price wasn't the issue at all.

Best wishes,
Fenella

Rep: Maren, Tobias, thanks for making time. Where do things stand?
Maren Lindgren (Director of Operations): Honestly, nowhere. I'll be brief. We've paused the project.
Rep: Can you tell me what happened?
Maren Lindgren (Director of Operations): Our CEO resigned two weeks ago. The board has an interim in place, and the interim has said no new platforms, no new contracts, until a permanent person is named. Could be spring. Could be next summer.
Tobias Abernethy (COO): It isn't a no. It's a not now. Everything that was in flight is stopped. We were also in the middle of a reorganisation of the regional managers, and that's frozen too.
Maren Lindgren (Director of Operations): Which is annoying, because it took us nineteen days to even get a demo scheduled, our fault, mostly, with people's calendars. And now the whole thing goes dark.
Tobias Abernethy (COO): We haven't gone anywhere else, I want to be clear. No competitor. We're staying on what we have.
Maren Lindgren (Director of Operations): Nothing was wrong with your product. And your quote was in line with what we'd budgeted. If it were up to me, I'd sign tomorrow. We're across seven states and I'd love to stop doing this by hand.
Rep: I understand. Can I follow up in the new year?
Maren Lindgren (Director of Operations): Do. I'll tell you if anything moves.

Rep: Maren, Nadia, thanks for joining. I got your message.
Maren Eastwood (Chief People Officer): Yeah. I'll say it plain. We're going with Corvane.
Rep: I appreciate you telling me. Can I ask why?
Maren Eastwood (Chief People Officer): Tax. We've got folks in five states. When I asked about a guy who works in Wisconsin and lives in Illinois, you said you'd have to check on reciprocity. When I asked about someone who moved from Michigan to Indiana in August, same. And the local stuff, Indiana counties tax residents, I think, that was another 'I'll get back to you.'
Nadia Abernethy (Head of People): I asked one too. Remote employee in Ohio, city tax. Nothing firm.
Maren Eastwood (Chief People Officer): The price was fine. I'd have paid it. I don't think it's even that different from Corvane. If your tax answers had been solid, we'd have been done weeks ago.
Nadia Abernethy (Head of People): And the sixteen days to get the demo was a long stretch. I'll mention it. But I wouldn't blame that.
Maren Eastwood (Chief People Officer): No. It's the taxes. I'm tired of being the person who finds out about problems in March.
Rep: Understood. Thank you.
Maren Eastwood (Chief People Officer): Sorry. It was a decent demo otherwise.

Subject: Our decision

Hi,

Thanks for all the time you and your team gave us. We've decided to go with Corvane.

The reason is state and local payroll taxes. We have employees in five states, and we needed clear answers on reciprocity, mid-year moves and local filings. We didn't get them from you with enough confidence. Pricing was not the issue.

The sixteen-day wait for the demo didn't help either, but it wasn't the deciding factor.

Thanks again,
Maren

Rep: Thanks for coming back, both of you. Last week was the overview, so today I'd like to dig into how payroll behaves across your nine states.
Amara Santangelo (People Operations Lead): Right. Concretely, then. We have 410 people, call it four hundred and ten, and about forty of them live in New Jersey but work in our Pennsylvania office. A dozen or so are the reverse. How does your system handle the reciprocity piece? Who's withholding for which state?
Rep: Good one. You can set a work state and a resident state per employee, and I believe it defaults to withholding for the work state, and then the employee files a form if they want it changed. For that specific New Jersey and Pennsylvania setup, I'd want to check with our tax team before I tell you how it's configured.
Amara Santangelo (People Operations Lead): Okay. That's the second time today I've heard 'check.' Delphine, you had the registration question.
Delphine Fairweather (HR Director): Yes. We open a site in Ohio in January, and Ohio has city-level income taxes, Columbus, Cleveland, they're not the same rate. Do you register us with the cities, or do we? And who files the quarterly city returns?
Rep: State registration we handle in onboarding. The city level, I'd have to get you an answer from our compliance group. I don't want to guess.
Delphine Fairweather (HR Director): And someone who relocates from Illinois to Colorado in July. Two states, one W-2, split wages. Do you generate that correctly?
Rep: We support it, but I'd want to confirm how the split gets reported.
Amara Santangelo (People Operations Lead): Look, price isn't what's bothering me. Your quote was about where we figured it'd be. It's that every tax answer ends in a follow-up. And one smaller thing: our accrual rules differ by office. California sick leave is front-loaded, Texas is a flat monthly accrual, and I don't see a way to set the rules per location. Is that coming?
Rep: Not something I can put a date on today.
Amara Santangelo (People Operations Lead): Understood. Let's regroup after we compare notes.

Rep: Bram, Linnea, thanks for joining. I know Linnea has to drop at the half hour, so let's get to the questions.
Bram Moreau (HR Director): Sure. We have 278 employees across eight states, and the tax side is where I keep getting nervous. Here's one. We hired a clinical coordinator in Oregon in March. First person there. Oregon has the statewide transit tax and the paid leave contributions on top of income tax withholding. Does your system register us for all of that, or do we do it ourselves with the state first?
Rep: So for the income tax piece we'd get the account set up. The transit and paid leave contributions, I'm honestly not sure which of those are automated for a first hire. I'd have to check.
Bram Moreau (HR Director): Okay. Second one. Corvane showed us a reciprocity grid, which employees live in Maryland, work in D.C., that sort of thing. We have about twenty of those. Where do I see that in yours?
Rep: There's a resident state and a work state field. How it resolves a Maryland-to-D.C. commuter, I'd want to confirm with our tax people. We'd have to check.
Linnea Petrakis (CFO): Can I jump in? I'm not worried about your pricing. It's in the range I budgeted, a little over, fine. What worries me is a notice from a state revenue department, six months from now, about an account nobody opened. Who owns that? Do you file or do we?
Rep: Depending on the plan, we file. I'd rather send you the exact scope in writing than answer from memory.
Linnea Petrakis (CFO): That's what I'd want. In writing, state by state, eight states.
Bram Moreau (HR Director): And if someone moves in September, say from Georgia to Tennessee, what happens to year-to-date wages?
Rep: Let me get back to you on that too.
Bram Moreau (HR Director): Okay. We'll talk internally.

Rep: Ravi, Teodoro, thanks. Where did the payroll walkthrough leave you?
Ravi Whitlock (Chief People Officer): Short version, we run six states, 455 people, a lot of seasonal. Teodoro has the specifics.
Teodoro Brannigan (Payroll Manager): Two things. We staff a ski property in Colorado. Denver and Aurora both have that monthly head tax on workers, the occupational privilege tax. Does your system calculate and remit it?
Rep: I know it handles state withholding. The local head taxes, I'd have to check.
Teodoro Brannigan (Payroll Manager): Second. Seasonal cook moves from our Florida kitchen to Georgia in June. No income tax, then income tax. Mid-year. What does the W-2 look like?
Rep: We'd have to check with the tax team on that one.
Ravi Whitlock (Chief People Officer): That's the pattern. Price is fine, by the way. It's higher than we pay now but I can defend it. I can't defend a guess about taxes.
Teodoro Brannigan (Payroll Manager): And honestly, budget review is next month. Our CFO might freeze new spending anyway.
Rep: Understood. I'll get you written answers on both.
Ravi Whitlock (Chief People Officer): Please.

Subject: Following up

Hi,

Thanks for the time with Teodoro and me. I'll be direct: we need confident answers on local head taxes in Colorado and on mid-year moves between Florida and Georgia, and we left the calls without them. Price wasn't the issue. Separately, our CFO is likely to pause new software spending after this quarter's review. We're going to hold off for now.

Ravi

Rep: Delphine, Beatrix, welcome. So, four states, around 400 people, right?
Delphine Delacroix (VP of People): 398, yeah, four states, Michigan, Indiana, Ohio and Illinois. And, okay, I'll just think out loud here because I've been circling this all week. Indiana. Indiana has county income taxes. Not city, county. And the rate depends on where the person lived on January first, and then where they work if they're in a different county. So if somebody moves in August, their rate doesn't change until next year. Does your system know that? Or do I fix it by hand?
Rep: Great question. So there's a place for local tax setup, and I know it handles state withholding well. The county piece for Indiana, I'm not sure how that works. I'd have to check.
Delphine Delacroix (VP of People): Right, right. And, hm, the other one is the Michigan cities. We have a plant near Grand Rapids and some people in Detroit, and I think the resident rate and non-resident rate are different, aren't they? So who's a resident of what? I mean, I could be wrong about that.
Rep: I'd want to confirm with our tax specialists before saying yes.
Beatrix Rourke (HR Director): Delphine, say the thing about cost so it's on the record.
Delphine Delacroix (VP of People): Oh, yes, cost. Cost is fine. Your number is fine. Corvane was a little lower but nothing I'd lose sleep over. It's that, if we get a county wrong, we find out in a notice. I don't want to find out in a notice.
Rep: I can get you a written answer on both.
Delphine Delacroix (VP of People): That would help, though I'm leaning toward the other one.

Rep: Hollis, Noor, thanks. Let's go to taxes, since that's what you flagged.
Hollis Rourke (Director of Operations): Yes. Nine states. 215 people. Noor?
Noor Abernethy (Payroll Manager): Two cases. First. We have staff in Kansas City, Missouri. And St. Louis. Both cities have an earnings tax. One percent. Employees pay it, we withhold it, we remit it. Do you do that?
Rep: I believe so. For the city earnings tax, I'd want to confirm.
Noor Abernethy (Payroll Manager): You believe so.
Rep: I'd have to check.
Noor Abernethy (Payroll Manager): Second case. A therapist moves from Massachusetts to New Hampshire in September. New Hampshire has no wage tax. Mass does. Which wages get taxed where? What shows on the W-2?
Rep: We handle moves, but I can't walk you through that exact scenario today.
Hollis Rourke (Director of Operations): Let me say this plainly. Price is fine. Your price is about what I thought. Corvane is a bit lower, I won't pretend otherwise. But I don't care. I care that when Noor asks a tax question, the answer is a maybe.
Noor Abernethy (Payroll Manager): Last one. Who registers us with the state tax agencies when we hire in a ninth state? Us or you? Our current vendor does it. They call us when it's done.
Rep: We guide you through registration. I'd want to confirm how much we do for you.
Hollis Rourke (Director of Operations): We need more than guidance. We're small. We don't have a tax team.
Rep: That's fair. I'll write up exactly what we file and what we don't.
Hollis Rourke (Director of Operations): Send it. But I'm not hopeful.

Rep: Nadia, Beatrix, good to talk again. Where are you?
Nadia Hollander (Office Manager): Decided, mostly. We're going with Tallyhold.
Rep: Okay. Can I ask what tipped it?
Nadia Hollander (Office Manager): Our broker. She's handled our renewals for years. She came to us and said here's the bundle, payroll and benefits admin together, one invoice, one portal. That's what she put in front of us. She does the renewal paperwork anyway, so it's easier if everything runs through her.
Rep: Sure. Did you compare it against what we showed you?
Nadia Hollander (Office Manager): A little. Yours looked good. I'm not going to say it didn't. But we've got 367 people in nine states and I don't have time to second-guess someone I trust. I trust our broker. If she says this is the right package, I follow her.
Beatrix Galbraith (HR Director): I'll be honest too. I sat in your demo, I liked it. But when the broker is the one calling about open enrollment every November, she's the person I call when something breaks. Having her tied to the system makes sense.
Rep: Understood. Is there anything on our side you'd want changed?
Nadia Hollander (Office Manager): No. It's not that. It's the bundle. Our broker put it in front of us, and we took it.
Rep: Fair enough. If that changes, we're here.
Nadia Hollander (Office Manager): Thanks. You were easy to work with.

Rep: Hollis, Soren, how's your week?
Hollis Ibarra (Office Manager): Long. Everyone's tired. Let's just get through the tax part, because Soren wouldn't let me skip it.
Soren Valdivia (Payroll Manager): Eight states, 441 employees. Case one. We have a nurse who lives in Vancouver, Washington and works in Portland. Washington has no income tax. Oregon does. Plus the Portland local stuff. Do you handle that?
Rep: Withholding for the work state, yes. The Portland local pieces, I'd have to check.
Soren Valdivia (Payroll Manager): Case two. Someone moves from Texas to Oklahoma in April. Nothing, then something. Mid-year. Do you split it?
Rep: We'd have to check on how that one is set up.
